index.title: An ALiBi Bias Stored with the Key
index.prompt: A causal ALiBi head adds -m(i - j) to the logit of query i against each key j <= i. To avoid building a row of biases at every decoding step, an engineer stores one extra number with each key when it enters the cache, b_j = m j, and adds b_j to that key's logit for every query i >= j. Nothing is added for the query's own position. How do the attention weights of query i compare with ALiBi's?
index.answer: They are the same, since for query i the stored bias differs from ALiBi's by m·i for every key alike, and softmax is unchanged by a shift shared by a whole row. The ALiBi bias is −m(i − j) = m·j − m·i. The part −m·i is the same for every key that query i sees, so it cancels between each exponential and their sum in the softmax, and only m·j is left. Causal ALiBi can therefore be folded into the cached key after all. It works because the penalty is linear in the offset. A learned T5 table b(i − j) has no such split.

index.title: A Sign Flipped in the Key Rotation

index.answer: The sum m + n, so two tokens a fixed distance apart score differently in different places. (R_m q)ᵀ(R_nᵀ k) = qᵀ R_mᵀ R_nᵀ k, and both factors are turns by negative angles, −mθ and −nθ, so they add to a turn by −(m + n)θ. index.title: Weights Trained with Another Pairing
index.prompt: RoPE code comes in two layouts. Both turn pair i by the angle mtheta_i, with theta_i = 10000^-2i/d. index.answer: The scores stay relative but differ from training, and moving rows i and i + d/2 of W_Q and W_K to rows 2i and 2i + 1 restores the trained scores. Any split into pairs keeps the score relative, so the loaded model still computes a function of n − m, but each feature now turns with a different partner and at a different speed than in training. Let P send coordinate i to 2i and coordinate i + d/2 to 2i + 1. Interleaved RoPE of P x is P times half-split RoPE of x, so with P W_Q and P W_K the queries and keys are the trained ones, both reordered by P, and a shared reordering leaves every dot product unchanged.

index.title: A Sliding Window Past the Training Length
index.prompt: A model with RoPE (base 10,000) was trained on sequences of 8,192 tokens. You run it over a 100,000-token server log and keep only the 8,000 most recent tokens in its cache, so each query attends to itself and the 7,999 tokens before it. Positions are counted from the start of the log, so they reach 99,999. What should you change about the positions?
index.answer: Nothing, because every score depends only on an offset between 0 and 7,999, and training produced every one of those offsets. By the cancellation, each pair's term depends on its speed times the offset between query and key, never on the positions themselves. With this cache the largest offset is 7,999, below the 8,191 of training, so every angle a score uses was met in training, on every pair. Large positions cost only rounding: in float32 an angle near 100,000 radians is stored to within about 0.004 radians. A window that has evicted the first tokens of the log can still fail, but not because of positions: many heads put much of their weight on the first few tokens, and those are gone.

theory.title: The Key a Rotary Head Prefers
overview: A toy attention head works in two dimensions and uses RoPE with an angle of $\theta = \pi/10$ per position, chosen for clean numbers (the real ladder starts at 1 radian). Before rotation its query is $\mathbf{q} = (1, 1)$ at every position and every key is $\mathbf{k} = (-1, 1)$. The head is causal, so the query at position $m$ sees only keys at positions $n \le m$. Write $r = m - n$ for how many positions back a key is.

prompt.p: Which key does the head score highest? Give the smallest $r$ at which the score is largest.

answer.p: Only the offset $n - m = -r$ matters, so the score is the query against the key turned by $-r\theta$. With $\varphi = r\theta$, turning $(-1, 1)$ by $-\varphi$ gives
and the dot product with $(1, 1)$ is

It rises from 0 at $r = 0$ through 0.618, 1.176, 1.618 and 1.902 to its maximum of 2 at $r = 5$, then falls again. The geometry says the same thing. The query points at 45 degrees and the key at 135 degrees, and turning the key back by 18 degrees per position lines it up with the query after $90 / 18 = 5$ positions. The maximum is $|\mathbf{q}|\,|\mathbf{k}| = 2$, the largest a dot product of these lengths can be.
Using $R_{m-n}$ instead turns the key the other way, through 270 degrees, and puts the maximum at $r = 15$.

prompt.p: Another key further back gets exactly the same top score. What is the next $r$ after the one from Part 1 with that score, and what does this say about a head with a single pair?

answer.p: The score $2\sin(r\pi/10)$ repeats every $2\pi/\theta = 20$ positions, so it is 2 again at $r = 25$, then at 45, 65 and so on. In the same way a key 20 back scores like the key at the query's own position.

With one pair the head cannot tell 5 back from 25 back. In real RoPE the pairs turn at speeds from 1 radian per position down to about $1/\text{base}$, with periods that do not line up, so a key 25 back differs from a key 5 back on most pairs and a head can aim at one offset without the repeats.

prompt.p: Porting RoPE to a new codebase, an engineer flips the sign of the sine terms in the key rotation only. Queries are still rotated by $R_m$, but the key at position $n$ is now rotated by $R_n^\top$, a turn of $-n\theta$. In two dimensions, what does the score $\langle R_m\mathbf{q},\ R_n^\top\mathbf{k}\rangle$ depend on?

choices.text: The sum m + n, so two tokens a fixed distance apart score differently in different places
choices.explain: (R_m q)ᵀ(R_nᵀ k) = qᵀ R_mᵀ R_nᵀ k, and both factors are turns by negative angles, −mθ and −nθ, so they add to a turn by −(m + n)θ. Positions 5 and 2 now score like positions 4 and 3, while positions 8 and 5, three apart like the first pair, score differently. choices.text: The offset n − m, as before, since a sign in the sine terms only mirrors the turn and turns still compose by adding angles
choices.explain: The flip is not harmless. The dot product already transposes the query's rotation, which is what turns R_mᵀ R_n into R_(n − m). The bug adds a second transpose, on the key, so the product is R_mᵀ R_nᵀ, a turn by −(m + n)θ, and the absolute positions no longer cancel.

choices.text: The offset m − n, so the head still sees relative position but reads it backward and attends forward instead of back

choices.text: Neither position, since R_m and R_nᵀ undo each other and the score is qᵀk wherever the tokens sit
choices.explain: R_m and R_nᵀ are inverses only when m = n. In the score the query's rotation appears transposed, as R_mᵀ, so the product is R_mᵀ R_nᵀ, a turn by −(m + n)θ, which is not the identity.

answer.p: (R_m q)ᵀ(R_nᵀ k) = qᵀ R_mᵀ R_nᵀ k, and both factors are turns by negative angles, −mθ and −nθ, so they add to a turn by −(m + n)θ. theory.title: Two Decay Rates in One Linear Head
overview: A linear attention head should weight the similarity of query $i$ and key $j \le i$ by

setup.p: a slow decay and a fast one together, so that it keeps both a long and a short memory.

prompt.p: If $w(i - j)$ could be written as $f(i)\,g(j)$, its value at offset 2 would be fixed by its values at offsets 0 and 1. What would $w(2)$ have to be? Compare it with the actual $w(2)$.

answer.p: As in the lesson, setting $j = i$ gives $g(i) = w(0)/f(i)$, so a factorizable weight satisfies $w(i - j) = w(0)\,f(i)/f(j)$. At offset 2, split the ratio into two steps of one:

Here $w(0) = 2$ and $w(1) = 0.8 + 0.5 = 1.3$, so a factorizable weight would need $w(2) = 1.69 / 2 = 0.845$. The actual value is $0.64 + 0.25 = 0.89$, so no single product $f(i)\,g(j)$ gives this weight.
The gap always goes this way for a sum of two decays: by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, $w(0)\,w(2) = 2(a^2 + b^2) \ge (a + b)^2 = w(1)^2$ for rates $a$ and $b$, with equality only when $a = b$.

prompt.p: Show that the head can still run as a recurrence, without the $n \times n$ matrix, and say what it costs compared with a head with one decay.

answer.p: Split the weight into its two terms. Each term is a single decay, which the lesson's recurrence handles, so keep one state per decay. Writing $\mathbf{u}_t = \varphi(\mathbf{k}_t)$ for the key's features,
The numerator and the denominator are both linear in the weights, so

The cost is two states instead of one: twice the memory and twice the update work per token, still fixed in size and still linear in the length. In general a weight that is a sum of $p$ decays needs $p$ states. A learned table over $L$ offsets can be matched by $L$ decays with distinct rates, since that is a Vandermonde system, but $L$ states of size $d \times d$ cost more than storing every key, so a table gains nothing.

theory.title: The Pairs NTK Scaling Carries Past a Full Turn
overview: A model uses RoPE with head dimension $d = 96$, so 48 pairs, and base 500,000: pair $i$ turns by $\theta_i = 500{,}000^{-2i/96}$ radians per position, for $i = 0, \dots, 47$. It was trained on 3,000-token sequences and is now run on 12,000 tokens, $s = 4$ times as long. As in the lesson, take the largest angle pair $i$ reaches in a context of $L$ tokens to be $L\theta_i$, and say that the pair completes a turn in training when $3000\,\theta_i \ge 2\pi$.

prompt.p: How many of the 48 pairs never complete a turn in training?

answer.p: Pair $i$ completes a turn when
So pairs 0 to 22 complete a turn (pair 22 has a wavelength of 2,572 tokens) and pairs 23 to 47 never do (pair 23 needs 3,380 tokens). That is $48 - 23 = 25$ pairs.

prompt.p: The context is stretched with NTK-aware scaling: the base becomes $500{,}000 \cdot s^{d/(d-2)}$ and the positions are left alone. Some of the pairs from Part 1 now complete a full turn somewhere in the 12,000 tokens, so they sweep every angle they never met in training. Which pairs are they? Give the highest-numbered one.

answer.p: With the new base, pair $i$ turns at
so its largest angle over 12,000 tokens is its training angle times a factor
which falls from about 2 near pair 23 to exactly 1 at pair 47. A pair completes a turn when that largest angle reaches $2\pi \approx 6.283$:

Pairs 23 and 24 pass $2\pi$, so the highest is pair 24. Pair 25 stops just short: its new wavelength is 12,208 tokens, a little longer than the context. Solving $3000\,\theta_i \cdot 4^{\,1 - 2i/94} = 2\pi$ for a real $i$ gives $i = 24.94$, which confirms the boundary.

The other pairs that never turned in training still meet some new angles, since their factor is above 1 for every $i < 47$, but only part of their unseen arc: pair 26 reaches 4.56 radians of 6.28, and pair 46 goes only from 0.01037 to 0.01068. Pair 47 has a factor of exactly $4^0 = 1$ and stops at its training angle, which is what the exponent $d/(d-2)$ is chosen to do. theory.title: The Position Term After the Projections
overview: Take one sinusoidal pair with speed $\omega$, so the position vector at index $i$ is $\mathbf{p}_i = (\sin \omega i,\ \cos \omega i)$. When the score is built from $W_Q(\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{p}_i)$ and $W_K(\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{p}_j)$, its position against position term is

setup.tex:
\mathbf{p}_i^\top M\,\mathbf{p}_j, \qquad
M = W_Q^\top W_K = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}.

prompt.p: Write $\mathbf{p}_i^\top M\,\mathbf{p}_j$ as a combination of the cosine and sine of $\omega(i - j)$ and of $\omega(i + j)$. Then take

and fix the offset $i - j$. Over all positions with that offset, what is half the gap between the largest and smallest values the term approaches? Assume $\omega / \pi$ is irrational, as it is for the speeds used in practice, so that $\omega(i + j)$ comes as close as you like to every angle.

answer.p: Write $s_i = \sin \omega i$ and $c_i = \cos \omega i$. The term is $a\,s_i s_j + b\,s_i c_j + c\,c_i s_j + d\,c_i c_j$, and the product-to-sum identities turn each product into a difference and a sum of angles:
Collecting terms,

answer.tex:
\mathbf{p}_i^\top M\,\mathbf{p}_j
= \tfrac{a + d}{2}\cos \omega(i - j) + \tfrac{b - c}{2}\sin \omega(i - j)
+ \tfrac{d - a}{2}\cos \omega(i + j) + \tfrac{b + c}{2}\sin \omega(i + j).

answer.p: For the given $M$ this is
The first two terms are fixed once the offset is fixed. The last two combine into one wave in $\omega(i + j)$ with amplitude

and as the positions slide along, $\omega(i + j)$ sweeps through every phase, so the term moves between the fixed part minus 2.5 and the fixed part plus 2.5. Two pairs of tokens the same distance apart can get position terms that differ by up to 5, while the part that does depend on the offset has amplitude only $\sqrt{3^2 + 0.5^2} \approx 3.04$.

prompt.p: For which matrices $M$ does the term depend on $i - j$ alone, whatever the speed $\omega$? Describe them geometrically.

answer.p: By Part 1 the term depends on $i - j$ alone exactly when the wave in $\omega(i + j)$ vanishes, so both of its coefficients are zero:
with $\rho = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. These are the rotations of the plane scaled by $\rho$, and for them the term is $a\cos \omega(i - j) + b\sin \omega(i - j)$.

The reason is geometric. Moving both positions along by $t$ turns both position vectors by the same rotation $A$, a turn through $\omega t$ radians, since $\mathbf{p}_{i+t} = A\,\mathbf{p}_i$, so the term becomes $\mathbf{p}_i^\top A^\top M A\,\mathbf{p}_j$. That equals the old term for every shift exactly when $M$ commutes with every rotation, and the matrices that do are the scaled rotations.

A trained $W_Q^\top W_K$ has no reason to satisfy the two equations $d = a$ and $c = -b$, so with an added encoding the position term is absolute in general. RoPE does not rely on the projections at all: it rotates the projected query and key, so the rotations meet directly inside the dot product.

choices.explain: This treats each pair's absolute angle as what the model reads, which it is not. A slow pair's term depends on its speed times the offset, at most 7,999 here, and that range of angles was covered in training for slow and fast pairs alike.

answer.p: By the cancellation, each pair's term depends on its speed times the offset between query and key, never on the positions themselves. With this cache the largest offset is 7,999, below the 8,191 of training, so every angle a score uses was met in training, on every pair. Large positions cost only rounding: in float32 an angle near 100,000 radians is stored to within about 0.004 radians. A window that has evicted the first tokens of the log can still fail, but not because of positions: many heads put much of their weight on the first few tokens, and those are gone.

answer.result: Nothing, because every score depends only on an offset between 0 and 7,999, and training produced every one of those offsets

theory.title: Which Angle Maps Keep Scores Relative
overview: A variant of RoPE in two dimensions turns the query at position $m$ by an angle $\phi(m)$ and the key at position $n$ by $\phi(n)$, for some function $\phi$ of the position. Positions are whole numbers $0, 1, 2, \dots$, and angles are compared modulo $2\pi$. RoPE itself is $\phi(m) = m\theta$.

prompt.p: Prove that the score $\langle R_{\phi(m)}\mathbf{q},\ R_{\phi(n)}\mathbf{k}\rangle$ is a function of $n - m$ for every $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ exactly when $\phi(n) = \phi(0) + n\theta$ modulo $2\pi$, for some constant $\theta$.

answer.p: Rotations are orthogonal and compose by adding angles, so the score is
**If.** With $\phi(n) = \phi(0) + n\theta$, $\Delta = (n - m)\theta$, a function of $n - m$. The constant $\phi(0)$ cancels.

**Only if.** Take $\mathbf{q} = (1, 0)$. With $\mathbf{k} = (1, 0)$ the score is $\cos\Delta$, and with $\mathbf{k} = (0, 1)$ it is $-\sin\Delta$. Both are functions of $n - m$ by assumption, and the cosine and sine together fix an angle modulo $2\pi$, so $\Delta(m, n) \equiv g(n - m)$ for some function $g$. In particular every step of one position turns by the same angle,
and adding these steps from 1 to $n$ gives $\phi(n) \equiv \phi(0) + n\theta$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

So the only freedom is the speed $\theta$ and a starting angle that cancels. Position interpolation, $\phi(m) = m\theta/s$, and NTK-aware scaling, which changes $\theta$ through the base, are both of this form, so both keep the scores relative. In $d$ dimensions the same argument applies to each pair on its own, so each pair needs an angle linear in the position, with its own speed.

prompt.p: A team proposes $\phi(m) = \ln(1 + m)$, so that angles grow more slowly far from the start of the text. Keys sit at or before the query. A query at position 19 and a key at position 9 give some score. Seen from a query at position 99, which key position gives the same score for every $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{k}$?

so by Part 1 it is not relative: at offset 1, the positions $(m, n) = (1, 0)$ give $\Delta = -\ln 2 = -0.693$ and $(3, 2)$ give $\Delta = -\ln(4/3) = -0.288$. For every $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ to give the same score, the angles must agree modulo $2\pi$. For keys at or before position 99 the angle lies between $-\ln 100 = -4.6$ and 0, a range shorter than $2\pi$, so the two angles must be equal:

The log map keeps ratios instead of differences. A key 10 back from position 19 looks like a key 50 back from position 99, so the head can no longer learn "the previous token" as one pattern: one position back means a smaller angle the further into the text it happens.

theory.title: When the Weights Stop Summing to One
overview: A linear attention head has a single pair of features, $d = 2$, and uses RoPE at the first rung of the ladder, $\theta = 1$ radian per position. Its feature map $\varphi = \text{elu} + 1$ is positive. Following Su et al., it rotates the features in the numerator only:

setup.p: In a stretch of text the features repeat: $\varphi(\mathbf{q}_t) = \varphi(\mathbf{k}_j) = (1, 1)$ at every position, starting from position 0. The values $v_j$ are numbers.

prompt.p: Every value is $v_j = 6$. Softmax attention would return 6 at every position. What does this head return at position 4? Give three decimal places.

answer.p: Each numerator term is $(1, 1)^\top R_{j-t}\,(1, 1)$. A rotation by $\alpha$ sends $(1, 1)$ to $(\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha,\ \sin\alpha + \cos\alpha)$, and the dot product with $(1, 1)$ is $2\cos\alpha$. The sine terms cancel because the query and key features are equal, so the term is $2\cos(t - j)$.
At $t = 4$ the keys sit at offsets 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0:
The denominator is $5 \times (1, 1)^\top(1, 1) = 10$, so

The weights on the five values are $-0.131, -0.198, -0.083, 0.108$ and $0.2$. They sum to $-0.104$, not 1, so five copies of the value 6 come back as $-0.62$: the output is not an average of the values.

prompt.p: A teammate rotates the denominator too, so that the weights sum to 1. The values are now $v_j = j$, that is 0, 1, 2 and 3. What does that head return at position 3? Give two decimal places.

answer.p: Every weight now has the same form on top and bottom, $2\cos(3 - j)$ over their sum:

The values run from 0 to 3, and the output is 27.31. The weights do sum to 1, but the terms of the normalizer have both signs and nearly cancel, so dividing by 0.268 blows the weights up. One position later the normalizer is $-1.039$, and with other features it can pass through 0 exactly.

prompt.p: Explain why rotating only the numerator is the safer of the two choices, and what it gives up.

answer.p: With positive features, every term of the plain denominator, $\varphi(\mathbf{q}_t)^\top\varphi(\mathbf{k}_j)$, is positive. The denominator can never be zero or change sign, and it grows with every key, so the division is always safe. The rotated denominator is a sum of terms of both signs, and nothing stops them from cancelling, as Part 2 shows.

What the plain denominator gives up is the meaning of an average. Its weights need not sum to 1 and can be negative, so a row of equal values does not come back unchanged, as Part 1 shows, and the output can leave the range of the values. Softmax attention has none of these problems, because its weights are positive exponentials divided by their own sum. Once the features are rotated their dot products can be negative, and no choice of denominator gets both properties back: the plain one keeps the division safe, the rotated one keeps the sum at 1.
